summary: This proposed standard defines a rendezvous extension for the Host Identity Protocol, extending HIP and its registration extension to start communication through rendezvous servers. These servers improve reachability when HIP nodes are multihomed or mobile.

eli5.summary: If your friend keeps moving, you leave a message with a forwarding desk that always knows where they are. This defines that desk for HIP.

questions: reach a mobile host with hip
what is a hip rendezvous server
how does hip relay the i1 packet
what is the hip from parameter
what is the hip via_rvs parameter
subtitle: How a HIP node that keeps moving stays reachable through a fixed relay that forwards first contact.

tldr.problem: A HIP node that changes IP addresses often cannot be found by peers who do not yet know where it is, and DNS updates propagate too slowly to help.
tldr.mechanism: The node registers its HITs and current IP addresses with a rendezvous server (RVS). Peers send the first HIP packet (I1) to the RVS, which rewrites its addresses and relays it to the node. The node then answers the Initiator directly.
tldr.outcome: RFC 8004 obsoletes RFC 5204 and only updates its references to the revised HIP specifications. It adds the FROM, RVS_HMAC and VIA_RVS parameters and the RENDEZVOUS registration type.

today: RFC 8004 is a Proposed Standard that obsoletes RFC 5204, and no later RFC is listed as obsoleting or updating it. Its only change from RFC 5204 was updating references to the revised HIP specifications.

sections.title: Why a Rendezvous Server
sections.content:
The Host Identity Protocol (HIP) lets nodes talk using host identities instead of IP addresses. A node that moves often is hard to contact, because a peer needs some IP address to send the first packet to. The architecture answers this with a third party, the rendezvous server (RVS), which acts as an initial contact point for its clients.

Clients are HIP nodes that use the HIP Registration Extension (RFC 8003) to register their HIT-to-IP-address mappings with the RVS. Other nodes then start a base exchange using the RVS's IP address, and the RVS relays that first contact so the exchange can complete.
sections.eli5: A rendezvous server is a forwarding desk. You hand it your first message, and it passes the message on to wherever your friend is today.

sections.title: How Relaying Works
sections.content:
Without an RVS, the Initiator sends an I1 packet straight to the Responder's IP address. With an RVS, the Responder has earlier registered its HITs and current addresses, and should record the RVS address in its DNS record using the HIP DNS resource record (RFC 8005). The Initiator looks up that address and sends the I1 to the RVS.

When the RVS sees an I1 whose HIT is not its own, it MUST check its registrations. If the HIT belongs to a client, it relays the I1 to the registered IP address. The Responder then replies with R1 directly to the Initiator's IP address, as read from the I1, and the rest of the base exchange (I2, R2) needs no further help from the RVS.

In this specification the client of the RVS is always the Responder. Letting a client start an exchange through its own RVS, for example for NAT and firewall traversal, is left to other documents.
sections.eli5: You give your first message to the desk, the desk hands it to your friend, and your friend writes straight back to you. The desk is not needed again.

sections.title: Rewriting and Relaying the I1
sections.content:
To relay an I1, the RVS rewrites the IP header. It replaces the destination address with one of the rendezvous client's addresses and MUST recompute the IP checksum.

Because of ingress filtering on the path from the RVS to the client, the RVS SHOULD also replace the source address (the Initiator's) with one of its own. Doing so hides the Initiator's address, so the RVS MUST append a FROM parameter carrying the original source address, protected by an RVS_HMAC keyed with the rendezvous registration integrity key.

The I1 carries no HMAC or SIGNATURE parameters, so HIP's end-to-end integrity checks are unaffected. The RVS SHOULD verify the I1 checksum before changing anything. Afterwards it MUST recompute the checksum over the updated HIP header and a pseudo-header with the new addresses, so the Responder can validate the checksum as is.
sections.eli5: The desk puts a new address label on the letter and staples on a note saying who really sent it, sealed so nobody can tamper with the note.

sections.title: The New Parameters
sections.content:
The RFC defines a registration type and three HIP parameters.

  • RENDEZVOUS is registration type 1 in the HIP Registration Extension, used to register for rendezvous service.
  • RVS_HMAC (type 65500) is a non-critical parameter that differs from the normal HMAC parameter only in its type code, which places it after the FROM parameter. It is keyed with the HIP-lg or HIP-gl integrity key established at registration. A valid one SHOULD be present on every packet between client and server and MUST be present when a FROM parameter is processed.
  • FROM (type 65498, length 16) holds an IPv6 address or an IPv4-in-IPv6 address. An RVS MUST add one whenever it rewrites the source address, appending it after any existing ones, along with an RVS_HMAC.
  • VIA_RVS (type 65502, variable length) holds the address of the RVS that relayed the I1. It exists for debugging, to help operators diagnose problems setting up an association through an RVS.
sections.eli5: There are three new labels: one that says who really sent the letter, one that proves the desk wrote it, and one the friend adds to say which desk passed it on.

sections.title: Packet Processing Rules
sections.content:
An RVS that gets an I1 whose destination HIT is not its own looks for a rendezvous registration by the HIT's owner. If it finds one, it relays the packet. If not, it drops it. It SHOULD treat an opportunistic I1 (one with a NULL destination HIT) as addressed to itself and not relay it, and an Initiator SHOULD NOT send such an I1 to a known RVS address unless it wants an association with the RVS itself.

A rendezvous client that receives an I1 MUST validate any RVS_HMAC. If it cannot be verified the packet SHOULD be dropped, and MUST be dropped if a FROM parameter is present. A Responder SHOULD drop opportunistic I1s that include a FROM parameter, since that shows the I1 was relayed.

When replying to a relayed I1, the Responder MUST append a VIA_RVS parameter to the R1. An Initiator receiving the R1 SHOULD match it to its I1 using HITs only. If it also checks IP addresses, the source address MUST be checked against the address in VIA_RVS.
sections.eli5: The desk only forwards mail for people who signed up, and it throws away anything it cannot match. Your friend ignores any letter whose seal looks wrong.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The RFC says it is hard to cover every threat from RVSs, because they matter at both the IP and HIP layers. They might allow redirection, amplification and reflection attacks at the IP layer, and man-in-the-middle attacks on the HIP base exchange.

If the Initiator already knows the Responder's host identity when it first contacts it via an RVS, it can verify the signatures in the base exchange, which protects against man-in-the-middle attacks. If it does not (an opportunistic Initiator), the public keys cannot be authenticated and defence is almost impossible. For simplicity, this specification does not allow establishing a HIP association via an RVS in an opportunistic manner.
sections.eli5: If you already know your friend's handwriting, you can tell a fake letter. If you have never seen it, a sneaky stranger could pretend, so the desk will not handle those cases.

sections.title: IANA Registrations
sections.content: RFC 5204 made the registrations that this document keeps: parameter types FROM (65498, length 16), RVS_HMAC (65500, variable) and VIA_RVS (65502, variable), and registration type 1, RENDEZVOUS. Their registry references now point to this document instead of RFC 5204.
